1247.title: John of Damascus
1247.hook: a monk and father of the Eastern church who defended icons
1247.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray before icons at home and in church, kissing them and lighting candles before them; Catholics honor statues and images in a similar way, while some Protestant churches keep worship spaces plain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maximus the Confessor: a human will saying yes in the garden, and a whole world at worship. Your line was a cosmic liturgy.

A ladder leans against a church wall. A man climbs it with a hammer and starts knocking a painted face of Christ off the plaster. Scenes like this are remembered from the fight in the Eastern empire over icons, the painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints; you met it in year three. One side said these pictures break the commandment and have to go. Far from the capital, a monk picked up his pen. Tradition says he had once served in the government at Damascus. His name was John. He wrote that icons were not only allowed. They told the truth about what God had done.

John starts by taking the objection seriously. The commandment in Exodus is real: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." He doesn't wave it away; he asks why it was given. In the old days, he says, God had no body and no face, so no one could picture the invisible. Then God's Son took on a human face. Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God." The first letter of John talks about what "we have seen with our eyes" and "our hands have handled." So, says John of Damascus, I'm not painting the invisible God. I'm painting the one people saw. Then the daring move behind today's line. The iconoclasts thought matter was too low to carry anything holy. John answers, in words close to these: I don't worship matter, I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake, and through matter worked my salvation. Wood, paint, bread, water, a human body: God uses all of it. So matter is not evil. Finally, he draws a line. Worship belongs to God alone. An icon receives honor, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love, and the honor passes through to the person shown. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor images this way. Some Protestant churches keep their walls plain, reading the commandment as a reason to leave images out of worship; others use art but don't venerate it. This path ranks none of them.

Set an icon in front of you, on paper or a screen, or a photo of a face you love if you have none. Look at the eyes first, then the hands, then the color, the gold or the plain background, the way you'd look at someone across a table, without analyzing. If you pray, let the looking become prayer.
John of Damascus. A monk who defended icons: because God's Son became human, the one people saw can be pictured, and the honor passes to him.
Your line: matter is not evil. Wood, paint and bread can carry something holy. See you tomorrow.

1248.title: Anselm's argument
1248.hook: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought
1248.howItsDone: Christians meet Anselm's argument in philosophy and theology classes, where it is still argued for and against; some also read his Proslogion as a book of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of Damascus and the icons: the maker of matter became matter. Your line was matter is not evil.

A monk is stuck. By his own account, he's been hunting for one single argument, short and complete, that would show God exists. It keeps slipping away. He tries to give up on it, and it won't leave him alone. Then one day it arrives, and he writes it down. His name is Anselm, and the surprise is where he puts the argument. Not in a lecture. In a prayer. The little book opens with Anselm talking to God, asking to see God's face. Only then, mid-prayer, does he make his move.

First, his reason for arguing at all. In words close to his: I don't seek to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand. Faith, looking for understanding. Then he turns to a psalm: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." He starts with a definition. God is something than which nothing greater can be thought. Even the fool understands those words, so the idea is at least in his mind. Now a painter. Before painting, the picture is in the painter's mind. After, it's in the mind and on the wall. Which is greater? The one that's real too. So if that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought existed only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, but real. And that can't be. So, Anselm concludes, it must exist in reality. Not everyone was convinced. A monk named Gaunilo wrote a reply on behalf of the fool: picture an island more perfect than any other; does that make it real? Anselm answered him, and the debate is still going among philosophers. But a few chapters later comes one more turn, the source of today's line. God, Anselm says, is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought. God is greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the argument isn't a fence around God. It ends at an edge, with more past it than the mind can hold.

Let your mind reach for the biggest, best thing it can hold: mountains, oceans, a love that never fails, the whole night sky. Notice that whatever you've got, you can still think of something greater, and rest there, at the edge of your thinking. If you pray, you can turn toward God the way Anselm did, talking first.
Anselm's argument. God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and, Anselm adds, greater than can be thought at all, an argument made inside a prayer.
Your line: greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the edge of thinking was a place to pray. That's today, done.

1249.title: Abelard and Heloise
1249.hook: a teacher who asked yes-and-no questions, and a brilliant abbess with her own theology
1249.carry: by doubting we come to inquiry
1249.howItsDone: Christians bring hard questions to Bible studies, classes, pastors and spiritual directors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm's argument, made inside a prayer. Your line was greater than can be thought.

A boy is missing. His parents search the city, and when they finally find him, he's in the temple, among the teachers. Luke says he was "both hearing them, and asking them questions." That boy is Jesus. Much later, a teacher in Paris named Peter Abelard points to this very scene to defend something risky: asking questions about the faith out loud. And among the people he taught was a young woman with a mind of her own, named Heloise.

Abelard made a strange book called Sic et Non, Latin for yes and no. He gathered sayings from the church fathers on one question after another, and set them side by side where they seemed to disagree. Yes, says one teacher. No, says another. He didn't settle the questions for his readers. In the preface, he gives reasons the fathers might seem to clash: a word used in different senses, a saying wrongly credited, a copy made badly, a teacher who changed his mind. Then comes today's line. By doubting, Abelard writes, we come to inquiry, and by inquiring we perceive the truth. And he points to Jesus himself: "Seek, and ye shall find." His own story was not peaceful. His love affair with Heloise ended in scandal and a violent attack on him, and both of them entered religious life. Some of his teaching was condemned in his lifetime. Heloise became an abbess, leading a community of nuns. Her letters to Abelard are fierce and honest. She argues that what makes an act good or bad is the intention of the heart, not only the outward deed. She asks him to write a rule fit for women, not one borrowed from men. And she sends him a list of hard questions about puzzling passages in the Bible, asking him to answer them for her nuns. Two people, both convinced that faith can bear honest questions. Christians still disagree about how far doubt should go. But the boy in the temple asked.

Let one real question rise, about faith, about God, about something you were taught and never quite understood. Say it plainly, inside, the way Heloise wrote hers down, and notice how it feels to hold a question without forcing it closed. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is.
Abelard and Heloise. A teacher who set the fathers' yes and no side by side, and an abbess with her own sharp theology, both sure that honest questions lead toward truth.
Your line: by doubting we come to inquiry. And by inquiring, Abelard says, we perceive the truth. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1250.title: The five ways
1250.hook: Aquinas offers five paths from the world to God, like motion needing a first mover
1250.howItsDone: Catholic schools and seminaries teach Aquinas's five ways as part of philosophy, and Christians of other churches meet them in theology and apologetics classes, where they are still debated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abelard and Heloise: yes and no side by side, and an abbess with hard questions. Your line was by doubting we come to inquiry.

A kettle sits on a stove. The water in it is cold, but it could be hot. Turn on the flame, and the heat that's really in the fire passes into the water, and the water starts to move. Bubbles. Steam. A whistle. Nothing mysterious about that. But a Dominican friar named Thomas Aquinas looked at moments exactly this ordinary, and asked where the chain of them leads. His answer opens with a plain sentence: the existence of God can be proved in five ways. And the first way starts with something moving.

For Aquinas, motion means any change at all: something that could be one way becoming that way. His own example is fire making wood hot. The wood can be hot; the fire actually is hot; so the fire moves the wood. The rule he draws: whatever is moved is moved by another. The wood by the fire, the fire by something else, all at once, like a hand moving a stick that moves a stone. That chain can't go on to infinity, he argues, or there would be no first mover, and so no other mover either. So there must be a first mover, moved by nothing, and this, he says, everyone understands to be God. The other four ways follow the same shape. Causes, which need a first cause. Things that come and go, which need something that doesn't come and go. Things more or less good and true, which point to what is best and truest. And things without minds that still act toward a goal, like an arrow flying straight because an archer aimed it. Two more details. Aquinas starts from the world, not from an idea in the mind; he wasn't persuaded that God's existence is obvious to us just from the definition. And he never says the five ways tell us everything. They show that God is, not what God is. Some truths about God, he says, reason can't reach without God revealing them. Paul wrote that God's invisible things are "clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Aquinas took him at his word, and started with a moving world.
screen: `THAT GOD IS, NOT WHAT GOD IS.`

The five ways. Aquinas's five paths from the world to God, starting with motion: whatever is moved is moved by another, back to a first mover.
Your line: everything moves. For Aquinas, the chain leads back to a first mover. Until tomorrow.

1251.title: Grace perfects nature
1251.hook: Aquinas: grace doesn't destroy what's human but completes it
1251.howItsDone: Catholic teaching quotes Aquinas's line that grace perfects nature; Christians of different churches give thanks for food, work, friendship and beauty as good gifts of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five ways: Aquinas following a moving world back to a first mover. Your line was everything moves.

A wedding in a village called Cana, and in the middle of the feast the wine runs out. Jesus tells the servants to fill the stone jars with water and take some to the man running the feast. He tastes it, and it's wine, and he calls the groom over, puzzled: "thou hast kept the good wine until now." Notice what Jesus didn't do. He didn't cancel the party, or swap the wedding for a prayer meeting. He took plain water, the stuff of an ordinary day, and made it better than anyone expected. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that fits that pattern.

Near the start of his Summa, Aquinas asks whether reason has any place in sacred teaching. His answer turns on a short phrase: grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it. Grace here means God's own gift, given freely. Nature means what we are as creatures: bodies, minds, appetites, friendships, the ability to think. Aquinas's point is that God's gift doesn't come to wipe all that out and start over. It comes to finish it. So reason isn't faith's enemy; it can serve faith. The same pattern runs through his whole picture of a human life. Courage, fairness, self-control: good human strengths, and grace doesn't cancel them. It lifts them toward faith, hope and love. Paul's letter to Timothy points the same way: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Christians weigh this differently. Catholic teaching draws on Aquinas's line. Lutheran and Reformed teaching stresses how deeply sin has wounded human nature, so that grace must heal before it can complete. Orthodox Christians speak of human beings being drawn into God's own life. Aquinas also says grace heals a nature wounded by sin, but his emphasis falls on completion. In his picture, grace doesn't take a person out of being human. It finishes the work.

Choose one ordinary good within reach: the taste of what you're drinking, sunlight on your hands, a song you love, the warmth of a blanket. Give it your full attention, without hurrying past it to something more spiritual. If you pray, receive it with thanksgiving, the way Paul's letter puts it; if you don't, simply let yourself enjoy it.
Grace perfects nature. Aquinas's line: God's gift doesn't destroy what's human, but completes it, the way water at Cana became good wine.
Your line: grace completes. Like plain water at Cana, made into good wine. Same time tomorrow.

1252.title: Thisness
1252.hook: Duns Scotus: each thing's unique thisness is loved by God
1252.howItsDone: Christians who follow Scotus's thought, especially in the Franciscan tradition, speak of God's love for each creature in its particularity; it shows up in prayer that names people one by one and in attention to the small, ordinary things of creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aquinas: grace doesn't wipe out what's human, it finishes it. Your line was grace completes.

Two leaves from the same tree. Same shape, same green, the same veins branching the same way. A botanist could file them under one name and be done. Hold them up to the window, though, and they aren't the same. One has a small tear near the stem; the other curls at the tip. This one, and that one. A Franciscan teacher named John Duns Scotus thought that difference went all the way down, and that God sees it and loves it. He had a word for it: thisness.

Medieval teachers wrestled with a hard question. If you and your neighbor share one human nature, what makes you you, and not just another copy of the human pattern? Some answered: the matter you happen to be made of. Scotus wasn't satisfied. He gave his answer a Latin name, haecceitas, which comes into English as haecceity, or thisness. Beyond the nature you share with everyone, he said, there is something that makes you this one. It isn't a leftover or an accident. It's real, and it belongs to you alone. His Latin is dense and careful, but the picture is easy to carry. God doesn't love humanity in general and each person as a sample of it. God knows the particular one. The Bible talks that way too. In Isaiah, God says to Israel: "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Not by category. By name. The psalmist says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb," and then, "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Made by hand, one at a time. And in John's Gospel the good shepherd "calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Loving people in general is easy. Loving this person, with this laugh and this stubborn habit, is harder. Some readers hear in Scotus a God who does the harder thing every time: this leaf, this sparrow, this face on the bus. Not one of them is a copy.
screen: `NOT ONE OF THEM IS A COPY.`

segments.voice: Pick something within reach, a mug, a stone, a leaf, your own hand, and look at it as if there were no other like it, because there isn't: the chip in the glaze, the crease across your palm that belongs to nobody else. When your mind starts filing it under a category, come back to this one. If you pray, you can thank God for this particular thing.
Haecceity. Thisness: what makes each thing this one and no other, and, for Scotus, part of what God knows and loves.
Your line: this one, loved. Not a sample, and not a copy. See you tomorrow.

1253.title: Ockham's razor
1253.howItsDone: Christian thinkers and teachers use the principle of not multiplying explanations in philosophy and theology, while holding that much of what they believe about God rests on revelation received in faith rather than on proof.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duns Scotus and haecceity, thisness. Your line was this one, loved.

The car is making a noise. A friend says it might be the transmission, or a curse, or a raccoon living in the engine. The mechanic opens the hood and finds a loose heat shield. Start with the simplest story that explains the noise; don't add raccoons you don't need. That habit has a name, and it belongs to a friar. William of Ockham was a Franciscan, like Scotus yesterday. His blade is called Ockham's razor.

One of Ockham's own Latin wordings goes like this: plurality is not to be posited without necessity. In plain English, don't multiply things without need. When two explanations cover the facts, keep the one with fewer moving parts. The rule later got a nickname, a razor, because it shaves away whatever does no work. Ockham used it on the philosophy of his day. Some teachers, he thought, had stacked invisible extras on top of the world, layer on layer, and he kept asking a plain question: do we need that? Often his answer was no. Yet the friar's razor didn't shave away God. For Ockham, much of what Christians hold about God isn't proved by clever argument at all. It rests on God's free revelation, received in faith. So the razor cleared clutter out of philosophy and left trust where it was. Jesus asked for plain speech too. Speaking about oaths in the Sermon on the Mount, he says, "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Say yes, mean yes, and stop. And when Martha was rushing around her house with guests to feed, he told her, "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful." Ockham's razor isn't a rule for faith. It's a rule for honest thinking: explain what you need to explain, and leave the raccoons out. That closes a week that walked from John of Damascus to Anselm, Abelard and Heloise, Aquinas and Scotus.

Bring to mind one story you've been telling yourself, why a friend hasn't texted back, why today feels off, and notice how many parts it has: hidden motives, secret plans, a whole plot. Then pick up the razor and hold the simplest explanation that fits what you actually know; maybe they're busy, maybe you're tired. If you pray, you can hand the leftover worry to God.
Ockham's razor. Don't multiply things without need: keep the simplest explanation that fits, and shave off the rest.
Your line: keep it simple. One thing is needful. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're Martha. guests are in the house, and your sister sits listening to Jesus instead of helping. you ask him to send her to the kitchen. what does he say?
options: "go on, Mary, help your sister."
"one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part."
"leave the guests; nobody needs to eat."
fork.reveal: he doesn't send Mary away. "thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful." many things, one thing.

chat.says: Doesn't Ockham's razor just shave God right out of the picture?
options: Not for Ockham. He used it on philosophy's clutter; faith in God rested on revelation.
Yes. Ockham used his razor to show that believing in God is simply unnecessary.
No, because Ockham's razor says the most complex answer is always the truest.
chat.meaning: Ockham's razor shaves away what does no work in an explanation. For Ockham, much of what Christians hold rests on God's revelation, received in faith.

Ockham.meaning: William of Ockham, a Franciscan friar and thinker

plurality.meaning: having many things; here, extra parts in an explanation

Sermon on the Mount.meaning: Jesus's long teaching in Matthew's Gospel

Martha.meaning: a friend of Jesus, busy with guests to feed

Franciscan.meaning: a member of the religious order of Francis of Assisi

sources.ref: Ockham, commentary on the Sentences (the parsimony principle)
